### Litany at the Exaltation of the Precious Cross[^699]

**1.** Have mercy on us, O God, according to Thy great mercy, we pray Thee, hear and have mercy: Let us all say.

**2.** Furthermore we pray for the most holy, ecumenical High Priest (Name), the Pope of Rome, and for our right-believing and God-preserved Emperor (Name), for their dominion, victory, endurance, peace, health, salvation, and remission of their sins, and that the Lord our God may especially prosper and help them in all things, and subdue beneath their feet every enemy and adversary: Let us all say.

**3.** Furthermore we pray for our most reverend Archbishop, Metropolitan Kyr (Name), and for our God-loving Bishop Kyr (Name), and for our spiritual fathers, and for all our brethren in Christ, for their health, and salvation, and remission of their sins: Let us all say.

**4.** Furthermore we pray for every Christian soul: for their health, and salvation, and remission of their sins: Let us all say.

**5.** Furthermore we pray for all who serve and have served in this holy temple: for their health, and salvation, and remission of their sins: Let us all say.

## Directory of Services of the Entire Year

### Notes

**1.** When any Service is transferred from a weekday to a Sunday, then the Service of the Saint occurring on that Sunday is transferred to the weekday of the Service transferred to Sunday.

**2.** In the Menologion, we give the names only of the Saints having a Service; the others we omit, since we do not need to commemorate them, but only the former.

**3.** The celebrant does not omit Services written in cinnabar letters; and he does not combine Services for the Dead with Festal Services having a cinnabar sign in the margin, but takes only the Festal Service with the intention for the dead.[^700]

**4.** Of the Services of the entire year, some are Immovable, that is, of the Menaion, and others are Movable, that is, of both Triodia and the Octoechos. We provide first the Directory of Immovable Services, then of the Movable.[^701]

**5.** Since the Services of the Menaion are of various classes, on this account, that the reader may understand what class of Service he is to undertake, we attach in the margin beside each Service one of the various signs defining the class of the Service, as follows:

- **`⊕`** Sign of a Feast of the Lord with an Afterfeast.
- **`⊕`** Sign of a Feast of the Mother of God with an Afterfeast.
- **`⊕`** Sign of a Feast with a Vigil without an Afterfeast.
- **`+`** Sign of a Polyeleos Feast.
- **`(:·`** Sign of a Feast for 6 with Great Doxology.
- **`(:`** Sign of a Feast for 6 with Small Doxology.
- **`(·`** Sign of a Feast for 4 with Epistle and Gospel at Liturgy.
- **`(`** Sign of a Feast for 4 with Troparion.
- **`(`** Sign of a Feast for 4 without Troparion.[^702]

### Number of Vigils of the Entire Year according to the Typikon of St. Sabbas[^740]

#### Chapter 3

We celebrate a vigil on every Sunday, so that the vigils of the whole year amount to 52. Vigils also take place on Feasts of the Lord in each month of them, as follows:

September: . . . . . 8, 14, 26,  
November: . . . . . . . . 21.  
December: . . . . . . . . 25.  
January: . . . . . . . 6, 17.  
February: . . . . . . . . 2.  
March: . . . . . . . . . 25.  
May: . . . . . . . . . . 8.  
June: . . . . . . . . 24, 29.  
August: . . . . . . 6, 15, 29.  
Ascension. — Together: . . . 68.  

If the Superior wills:  
November: . . . . . . . . 13.  
December: . . . . . . . . 5.  
January: . . . . . . . . 20.  
That of the Saint according to the monastery, in which [the feast] takes place without fail also in his monastery.  
There are also Litiyas that take place, if the Superior wills.

# Typik of Fr. Isidore Dolnytsky (1899) — Cohort 29


---

[Leaf p561 / Page 559]

## Directory of Movable Services

### Of the Lenten Triodion

#### Sunday of the Publican and the Pharisee
In the six days from Monday until the Saturday of the Prodigal Son, the Triodion has nothing, but only the Octoechos and the Menaion. — Fast-free week.

#### Sunday of the Prodigal Son
**1.** In the five days from Monday until Meatfare Friday, the Triodion has nothing, but only the Octoechos and the Menaion.  
**2.** Meatfare Saturday: For the Dead (All Souls), without the Menaion.

#### Sunday of Meatfare
##### Of the Dread Judgment
**1.** The Service of Cheesefare Week is Penitential, as a Forefeast of the Great Forty Days.  
**2.** On Monday, Tuesday, and Thursday, the Triodion has little, and the Octoechos and the Menaion hold the rest.  
**3.** On Wednesday and Friday, the Triodion has the fuller Fasting Service.  
**4.** **(:** Cheesefare Saturday: To the Holy Ascetics.

#### Sunday of Cheesefare
##### Adam’s Expulsion from Paradise
**1.** In the five days from Monday until Friday of the 1st Week of the Fast, the Service is Fasting. — With Monday begins the Great Forty Days.  
**2.** 1st Saturday of the Fast: Great Martyr Theodore the Recruit (Tyro).

---

[Leaf p562 / Page 560]

#### 1st Sunday of the Fast
##### Orthodoxy: Against the Iconoclasts
**1.** In the five days from Monday until Friday of the 2nd Week of the Fast, the Service is Fasting.  
**2.** From Monday and downward, we sing at Compline the Canons of the Saints of the Menaion that will occur from Lazarus Saturday until Thomas Sunday, both inclusive.  
**3.** 2nd Saturday of the Fast: Service to the Martyrs, Hierarchs, and all Saints, likewise for the Deceased, according to the Typikon of Alleluia Saturdays, with the Service of the ordinary Saint of the Menaion. Thus it takes place also on the 3rd and 4th Saturdays of the Fast.

#### 2nd Sunday of the Fast
##### Nameless, Penitential
**1.** In the five days from Monday until Friday of the 3rd Week of the Fast, the Service is Fasting.  
**2.** 3rd Saturday of the Fast: Service of an Alleluia Saturday, as that of the 2nd.

#### 3rd Sunday of the Fast
##### Veneration of the Precious Cross
**1.** In the five days from Monday until Friday of the 4th Week of the Fast, the Service is of the Cross-Veneration.  
**2.** 4th Saturday of the Fast: Service as on the 2nd and 3rd of the Fast.

#### 4th Sunday of the Fast
##### Nameless, Penitential
At discretion, also the Service to Saint John of the Ladder (Climacus).  
**1.** On Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and Friday of the 5th Week of the Fast, the Service is Fasting.

---

[Leaf p563 / Page 561]

**2.** On Thursday of the 5th Week of the Fast: Penitential Service of the Great Canon, with prostrations.  
**3.** 5th Saturday of the Fast: Of the Akathist.

#### 5th Sunday of the Fast
##### Nameless, Penitential
At discretion, also the Service of Venerable Mary of Egypt.  
In the five days from Monday until Friday of the 6th Week of the Fast, the Service is Fasting.

### Of the Flowery Triodion (Pentecostarion)

#### 6th Saturday of the Fast: Of Lazarus
The Canons of the Saints that occur in the ordinary course of the Menaion from this Saturday until Thomas Sunday have been pre-sung at Compline from Monday of the 2nd Week of the Fast downward.

#### ⊕ 6th Sunday of the Fast: Palm Sunday (Flowery)
Feast of one day, with a Vigil.  
**1.** On Great Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday: Passion-Penitential Service, as a Forefeast of Christ's Sufferings.[^741]  
**2.** On Great Thursday: The Mystical Supper, and the beginning of Christ's Passion.  
**3.** On Great Friday: The Passion of Christ.  
**4.** On Great Saturday: The Laying of Christ in the Tomb.

#### ⊕⊕ Sunday of Pascha: THE RESURRECTION OF CHRIST
Feast of thirty-nine days.  
**1.** From Monday until Bright Saturday inclusive, we sing the entire Service to Pascha.

---

[Leaf p564 / Page 562]

**2.** On Monday and Tuesday we abstain from labor and are present at divine services; and during the entire week we are permitted meat (fast-free).

#### ⊕⊕ 2nd Sunday after Pascha: Antipascha: Of Thomas
Feast of seven days, with a Vigil.  
Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, and Saturday: Within the Feast of Thomas Sunday, with the Menaion.

#### 3rd Sunday after Pascha: Of the Myrrh-Bearers
Feast of seven days.  
Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, and Saturday: Within the Feast of the Myrrh-Bearers, with the Menaion.

#### 4th Sunday after Pascha: Of the Paralytic
Feast of three days.  
**1.** Monday and Tuesday: Within the Feast of the Paralytic, with the Menaion.  
**2.** Wednesday of Mid-Pentecost: Feast of eight days, without a Vigil, and without a Polyeleos.

#### 5th Sunday after Pascha: Of the Samaritan Woman
Feast of four days.  
**1.** Monday and Tuesday: Within the Feast of Mid-Pentecost; but the Service of the Samaritan Woman is deferred until the Feast of Mid-Pentecost is concluded (Apodosis).  
**2.** **(:** Wednesday: Apodosis of Mid-Pentecost.  
**3.** Thursday, Friday, and Saturday: Within the Feast of the Samaritan Woman.

---

[Leaf p565 / Page 563]

#### 6th Sunday after Pascha: Of the Blind Man
Feast of four days.  
**1.** Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday: Within the Feast of the Blind Man; and on Wednesday also the ⊕ Apodosis of Pascha, and the Forefeast of the Ascension.  
**2.** **⊕⊕** Thursday: ASCENSION. Feast of nine days, with a Vigil.

#### 7th Sunday after Pascha: Of the Holy Fathers
**1.** Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday: Within the Feast of the Ascension.  
**2.** **(:** Friday: Apodosis of the Ascension.  
**3.** Saturday for the Dead (All Souls), according to the Meatfare Typikon, here on page 363.

#### ⊕⊕ Sunday of Pentecost: DESCENT OF THE HOLY SPIRIT
Feast of seven days, with a Vigil.  
**1.** Monday of the Holy Spirit (and the Feast of the Holy Trinity, at discretion): Abstinence from labor, with attendance at divine services.  
**2.** Dispensation for meat (fast-free) throughout the entire week.  
**3.** **(:** Saturday: Apodosis of the Descent of the Holy Spirit.

#### 1st Sunday after Pentecost: All Saints
Here is the end of the ancient Triodion.  
**1.** With this Sunday begins the series of Sunday Matins Gospels and daily Liturgy Gospels.  
**2.** On Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday, the Triodion has nothing.  
**3.** **⊕⊕** Thursday: OF THE EUCHARIST (Corpus Christi). Feast of eight days. The Vigil is transferred to Sunday.

---

[Leaf p566 / Page 564]

#### 2nd Sunday after Pentecost: Vigil of the Eucharist
**1.** With this Sunday begins the cycle of the Tones.  
**2.** **(:** On Thursday: Apodosis of the Feast of the Eucharist.  
**3.** **+** On Friday: Compassion of the Most Holy Theotokos. Feast of one day, with a Polyeleos; and with this is the end of the new Triodion.

### Of the Octoechos

| Day | Service | Dedication |

### Explanation of the Tablet

**1.** The Tablet contains 35 Columns of the Sundays of the entire year according to the number of the 35 Boundary Keys, and the 35 Paschal days corresponding to them.

**2.** At the head of the Tablet, that is, in its 1st horizontal row, stand all 35 Boundary Keys; and beneath each key extends a row, or Column, of the Sundays of the entire year, with an indication of the day of the month within whose boundaries these Sundays occur, and their numbers or titles. And the months are written outside the column, on the left, separated from one another by horizontal, red, step-like lines; the day of the month is written inside the Column, while the number or title of the Sunday is written outside the Column, on the right of the Tablet.

**3.** In the 7th row stand all 35 days on which the Sunday of the Publican may occur, with which the Triodion begins.

**4.** In the 8th row stand all 35 Paschal days written in cinnabar (red), corresponding to the 35 Boundary Keys.

**5.** In the 5 rows contained between the Publican and the Boundary Keys, stand all 5 Sundays that can occur between Theophany and the Publican, namely, the Sunday after Enlightenment (Theophany), and the 4 last ordinary Sundays (29th, 30th, 31st, 32nd). However, since not all these Sundays always take place, as we explained on page 159 (for this depends on the earliness or lateness of Pascha), on this account in these 5 rows certain spaces are found blank, which signifies that then the Sundays corresponding to them on the right of the tablet have no place. For example, under the Boundary Key 1 (A), all spaces are blank; it signifies, therefore, that of

---

[Leaf p580 / Page 581]

these 5 Sundays not a single one is then taken, but immediately after Theophany the Triodion begins.

**6.** Of the Triodion Sundays we have set down only three, that is, the central one, which is Pascha, and the two extreme ones, namely, that of the Publican, and that of All Saints; but the other intervening ones we have omitted, since it is easy to keep them in memory even without the Tablet, for they usually have special titles, and proper Services corresponding to the titles.

**7.** On the Sundays preceding that of the Publican we have set down neither the Tone nor the Sunday Gospel, for these depend on the preceding Pascha, and on this account one must seek them at the end of the Tablet in the boundaries of January and February under the Boundary Key of the preceding Pascha.

**8.** Beside certain Sundays, red Latin letters are placed. This signifies that then, together with the Gospel of that ordinary Sunday, another Gospel of a certain Sunday of the 10 special ones of the Menaion is also to occur, which we have set down at the end of the Tablet with corresponding Latin letters.[^743]

**9.** After this, if one desires to know which Sundays in a given year ought to be taken between Theophany and the Publican, let one seek first of all the Boundary Key of the coming Pascha, according to the Directory of Tablet I or II, and under it in Tablet III one will find those Sundays; only, if it is a leap year, adhere to the Column immediately following. And if one desires to know which Sunday, Tone, and Sunday Gospel is to be taken on any of the Sundays after the Descent of the Holy Spirit, then know—

<!-- END COHORT 1899_dolnytsky_typikon_cohort29 -->

---

<!-- START COHORT 1899_dolnytsky_typikon_cohort30 -->

# Typik of Fr. Isidore Dolnytsky (1899) — Cohort 30


---

[Leaf p581 / Page 582]

-ing known the Boundary Key of that year, and having gone down along its Column to the month and day of the Sunday, proceed from it along the horizontal row to the right side of the Tablet, and you will find all these things.

**10.** Concerning the Apodosis of the Meeting, which we have set down in the last row of numbers of the Tablet, know that under Key 1 (A), where we have placed the number 0, it signifies that then there is no Apodosis; under the Keys from 17 (R) even unto the end, the Apodosis occurs on February 4; under the other Keys it occurs on various days according to the distinction of the different Keys; only in a leap year adhere to the Column immediately following. But the Boundary Keys ought to be observed from the coming Pascha.

## Rubric Concerning the Holy Doors and the Curtain of the Iconostasis

The Holy Doors, according to the rubric of the Greek *Euchologion*, are opened only: *at the beginning of Great Vespers, when the Priest alone incenses; at all the Entrances, namely of Vespers and of the Liturgy, and of the Holy Gospel. Likewise it is opened also from "With the fear [of God]..." until the completion of the Divine Liturgy.* [Greek: εἰς τὴν ἀρχὴν τοῦ μεγάλου Ἑσπερινοῦ, ὅτε θυμιᾷ μόνος ὁ Ἱερεὺς, εἰς τὰς εἰσόδους πάσας, ἤγουν τῶν Ἑσπερινῶν καὶ τῆς Λειτουργίας, καὶ τοῦ ἁγίου Εὐαγγελίου. Ὡσαύτως ἀνοίγεται καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ Μετὰ φόβου... μέχρι τῆς συμπληρώσεως τῆς θείας Λειτουργίας.]

The Curtain, however, according to the current custom of the Athonite Monasteries, is opened at the Liturgy upon the completion of the Proskomide, and after the Great Entrance it is closed, and at *Especially* (*Izryadno*) it is opened, and after *And may the mercies* (*I da budut*) it is closed, and at *With fear* (*So strakhom*) it is opened, and remains open until the end of the Liturgy.[^744] According to the former custom of the Holy Mountain of Athos, when a single Priest celebrates, that is, without a Deacon, the curtain, having been closed after the Great Entrance, is not opened until the completion of the Communion. Furthermore, it remains open at Vespers and at Matins with the First Hour, and at the Moleben. But when the Hours are chanted without the Liturgy, it is opened for the Reading of the Epistle, and is closed after the Dismissal of the Typika.[^745]

According to the rubric placed at the end of our Apostoly, and in our earlier Sluzhebnyky, as also in certain Greek Sluzhebnyky in Goar, the daily Antiphons *It is good to give praise* are appointed also on Sundays, with only the Sunday refrain at the 3rd Antiphon, even as the Italo-Greeks also use. The general Greek Sluzhebnyky appoint the Typika (*Izobrazitelna*) on Sunday, and the Oktoechoi likewise on weekdays; for in them Stichera on the Beatitudes are appointed daily, which presuppose the Typika. In this diversity of rubrics let each church preserve its own custom; among us, however, the rubric of the Synod is observed. During the Synod some contended vigorously, asserting that to take the Antiphons daily in place of the Typika is contrary to our Rite; for the daily Antiphons are cited not only by the aforesaid Sluzhebnyky and Apostoly, but also by Greek Anagnostika and the Russian Typikon in ch. 21, and by St. Sophronius, Patriarch of Jerusalem in the 7th century, who in his *Explanation of the Divine Liturgy* (*Spicileg. Rom.*, tom. 4, nn. 12, 13, 14, Rome, Propaganda, 1840) makes no mention whatever of the Typika, but only of the Antiphons *It is good to give praise*. Concerning the Typika (*Izobrazitelna*), however, we consider that they were composed for the case when there was no Divine Liturgy. For from the beginning the majority of monastics consisted of laymen who could not celebrate the Liturgy; and for this reason, after the image of the Divine Liturgy, the Order of the Typika was instituted for their use; wherefore the Synod also restricts them to days on which there is no Divine Liturgy, and that their memory may be preserved, only to monasteries. To use the Antiphons is equally good as the Typika, if the latter are taken in their entirety; but if of each Psalm only a single verse is taken and without Stichera on the Beatitudes, as they commonly use, then it is better to use the Antiphons. Moreover, the full Typika are long, and present times are times of abbreviation.
[^68]: Our Sluzhebnik in the order of the Sundays which are from the 2nd to the 9th after the Descent of the Holy Spirit.
[^69]: Moscow Typikon in ch. 3, and Peremyshl p. 79.
[^70]: The Troparia and other variable parts of the Divine Liturgy, according to the earlier Typikon, were not to be taken only of the Sunday, but also to the Saint, if he had anything. (For example: Chapter of Mark 68 and 74; and our Menaion September 6, if it occurs on Sunday). For in the earlier Typika the Saint sometimes did not have a Troparion, sometimes not even a Kontakion; sometimes he had only a Troparion or only a Kontakion, and sometimes also a Prokimenon-Alleluia, and Epistle and Gospel, and Communion Hymn. Nevertheless, since among us Troparia and Kontakia were added late to all Saints who are in order in the Menologion, for this reason Services to a Non-Polyeleos Saint are not taken at the Divine Liturgy; the Greeks, however, in the case of a Saint having an Epistle and Gospel on Sunday, began to take the Epistle only to the Saint, but the Gospel only of the Sunday. (New Constantinopolitan Typikon 1851, e.g. September 6).

For the sake, then, of distinguishing Sunday from weekdays, at Small Matins it is more fitting to use the second: *For sanctified is*, although the first, *For blessed is* (*Ὅτι εὐλόγηται*), would not be ill used either, since in Greek Books we find only this single exclamation, without distinction of the day. Nevertheless, this rubric of the Universal Church is not maintained by the Patriarch of Constantinople, called ecumenical, nor the Churches subject to him, which (according to the testimony of Archbishop Benjamin of Neapolis, who lived in Constantinople and on Mount Athos, and who in our times entered Church communion) have the custom, as also in monasteries, to take the Epistle and Gospel only of the day, if the Saint does not have one, but if he has, then only to the Saint; and in other respects they follow the new Constantinopolitan Typikon, printed at the Patriarchal Typography in 1851, stamped with the Patriarchal seal, and honored by the subscription of all the Patriarchs and the Greek Bishops subject to them, in which Typikon, wherever the rubric appoints two Epistles and Gospels, there is appointed only a single Epistle and Gospel, that is, the Epistle of the one Service, and the Gospel of the other Service. Thus, for example, on October 26 and November 21, when they occur on a Sunday, and on May 8, St. John the Theologian, when it occurs on Ascension.

[^198]: Concerning the Festal commemoration at the Dismissal in an Afterfeast, we find nothing in the Greek Typika. From the rubrics of the Slavonic Triodia and the *Tserkovne Oko* and the Moscow Typikon, it could be concluded that the Festal commemoration is to be taken only on the festive day of the Feast itself, and on its Apodosis. For it commands to take the Paschal Dismissal throughout Bright Week, each day of which has the form of the Divine Services of the very day of Pascha, and afterwards commands to take it at the Liturgy of the Apodosis of Pascha. Nevertheless, we find today the common custom to make the Festal commemoration also on the other days of the Afterfeast, which has in its favor the rubric of the Sluzhebnik printed in Stratyn under Bishop Gedeon Balaban of Lviv in 1604, eleven years before the *Tserkovne Oko*, which has as follows: "Know that Festal Dismissals are said from the day of the Feast even unto the Apodosis of the Feast, on all days" (p. 537). And this could be used in the Afterfeast of a Feast of the Mother of God; however, let the words "today" and "festively" be omitted. In Afterfeasts of the Lord, however, it is better to omit the Festal commemoration on Sunday, as it does not harmonize well with the Resurrectional commemoration, which ought to occupy the first place. For example, in the Afterfeast of the Nativity of Christ it would be: "He who rose from the dead and was born in a cave in Bethlehem of Judea and lay in a manger for the sake of our salvation, Christ our true God." On weekdays besides Sunday, the Festal commemoration can be used without obstacle, because then the Festal Service supplants the Service of the Oktoechos, and therefore in place of the commemoration of the daily Service, that is, of the Oktoechos, the commemoration of the Festal Service is well taken. Some on Sunday omit the Resurrectional commemoration and take only the Festal one; nevertheless, these have against them our Sluzhebnyky, which on the Sunday of the Holy Fathers within the Feast of Ascension, before Pentecost, appoint the Resurrectional commemoration.

Those which are silent concerning it are 4 Vatican manuscript Typika, placed in the Library Catalogue under Nos. 784, 101, 782, and 785: the 1st from the year 1317, the 2nd 1373, the 3rd of unknown year, yet of the 14th century, the 4th of the 14th or 15th century. Those which exclude it are: the Moscow Typikon of 1859 for the use of the All-Russian Church with the approval of the Directing Synod; the *Tserkovne Oko* and the ancient manuscript Typikon which we possess; for although these two Typika are silent concerning the Litany on Cheesefare Sunday, nevertheless on the 1st Sunday of the Fast they exclude it, for immediately after the Prokimenon they say: "After this, **'Vouchsafe, O Lord'**." We, however, deem that the Typika which omit the Litany are more reasonable: for at all other Lenten Vespers and Matins that Litany is not present, but after the Troparia in its place is appointed **"Lord, have mercy"** 40 times, and **"He that is blessed"** (or something else) with the prayer **"O Heavenly King"**. Since, therefore, Vespers of these Sundays is also Lenten, for this reason on them there ought not to be a Litany, all the more since the prayer **"O Heavenly King"** can stand in place of the petitions which are in the Litany. And that not every Entrance draws after itself the Litany **"Let us all say"**, this is evident from the Typikon of the Finding of the Precious Head of the Forerunner when it occurs on Lenten days, there being no Liturgy of the Presanctified; for then also the *Tserkovne Oko* in Chapter Mark 92 says: "We do not say **'Let us all say'**, but **'Vouchsafe, O Lord'**," and our and the Russian Typika say: "Reading of the day and of the Forerunner, and immediately **'Vouchsafe, O Lord'**."

## Cohort 21 Footnotes

[^542]: For what reason the commemoration of the Holy Great-Martyr Theodore is celebrated on this Saturday, Nilles shows in *Kalendarium Manuale (Heortologion)*, writing thus: "At Constantinople the cult of the same Holy Martyr was very celebrated on account of the miracle of the *kolyva* (*τῶν κολλύβων*), whose anniversary commemoration is celebrated on the first Saturday of Lent by an established feast of its own. Julian the Apostate wishing indeed to compel the Constantinopolitans to eat idol-meats, and for this reason ordering in the year 362 that all things for sale in the marketplace be secretly tainted and polluted with the blood of sacrifices, Saint Theodore the Tyro, appearing by night in a vision to the Bishop of the royal City, commands that another food supply, called by the Euchaitian word *kolyva* (*κόλλυβα*), be furnished to the poor." (At Feb. 17, p. 106). And *kolyva* (*κόλλυβα*), according to the words of Nikephoros Kallistos, is boiled wheat. Thus also the Synaxarion of this Saturday has it.

[^559]: The Akathist Order, that is, the Non-sitting [Hymn], is chanted in memory of the thrice-repeated deliverance of Constantinople from the invasion of the heathen, and this by the intercession of the Great Mother of God, whose precious Robe, brought from Jerusalem and placed in the Blachernae Church by Saint Pulcheria, and her icon under the name Hodegetria, painted according to the opinion of the Greeks by Saint Luke, they carried around the City, calling upon her aid. The first invasion was under the Emperor Heraclius (reigned 610 to 641) by the Persian army under the command of Satrap Sarbaros, and likewise by the Scythian army under the command of the Khagan. It was defeated partly by a small number of Christian Warriors who went out against the adversaries from the Church of the Most Holy Theotokos; and partly by a violent tempest at sea, which destroyed them with their ships. The second invasion was 36 years later, namely under Constantine Pogonatus (668–685), and ended partly by pestilence among the soldiers, and partly by a tempest at sea, when they were returning home. The third was under Leo the Isaurian (717–741), and ended by a tempest at sea, and famine, and the division of their forces against the Bulgars, by whom they were crushed. (*Synaxarion* of this Saturday, concerning which also Nilles, *Kalendarium Manuale*, Vol. 2, p. 152).
[^560]: Apart from the initial Kontakion, **"To thee, the Champion Leader"** (*Взбранной Воеводе*), the rest of the Akathist consists of 12 Ikoses and 12 Kontakia, together of 24 clauses, according to the number of the 24 letters of the Greek Alphabet, by which each clause in the Greek text begins in order.
[^561]: In the Patriarchal Church of Constantinople they sing the Akathist not at Matins, but earlier at Little Compline, namely at **"It is truly right"** the 1st Stasis the Patriarch himself; the 2nd, after the 3rd Ode of the Festal Canon, the Metropolitan of Caesarea; the 3rd after the 6th Ode, the Metropolitan of Ephesus; the 4th after the 9th Ode, the Metropolitan of Heraclea. (*New Typikon of Constantinople*).
[^562]: The Greek Triodion does not appoint even a single censing. It would be better for us to cense only once, at the beginning.

Likewise, by custom (and not by Church Typikon) of the Greeks independent of the Patriarchate of Constantinople, the entrance into the church takes place through questions and answers borrowed from Psalm 23: **"Lift up your gates, ye princes, and the King of glory shall enter in,"** etc. And when it is said: **"The Lord of hosts, He is the King of glory,"** then the doors are opened, and the entrance into the church takes place. *Μάλιστα ἐπικρατεῖ τὸ ἔθος εἰσέρχεσθαι διὰ τῶν ἐρωταποκρίσεων: Ἄρατε πύλας, καὶ ἀνοίγειν τὴν θύραν μόνον εἰς τὸ Κύριος τῶν δυνάμεων, αὐτός ἐστιν ὁ βασιλεὺς τῆς δόξης* [Especially does the custom prevail of entering through the dialogues: "Lift up the gates," and opening the door only at "The Lord of hosts, He is the King of glory"], says a dispatch from Corfu. This custom we found also among the Greek-Melkites and the Vlachs, and likewise in various Churches of the Latin Rite, concerning which Nilles writes thus: *Aliae ecclesiae contra, magna ex parte Graecos imitantur, ac proinde horum caeremonias hic breviter describimus. Ad repraesentandum igitur Christi triumphum de inferno delatum, summo mane ante Matutini recitationem ordinatur processio, in cuius reditu inveniuntur ecclesiae portae clausae: tunc episcopus vel sacerdos illa psalmi verba Tollite portas etc. profert, et ex interiori parte clericus vel alius cantor respondet: Quis est iste rex gloriae etc. Tandem post contentionem celebrans percutiens valvas, intonat: Surrexit Christus, et statim ecclesiae janua expanditur. Tunc altum extollit cereum triangulum, quem in manu gestat, quemque ipsi Τρικήριον appellant; quam eandem caeremoniam populus assistens facit cum lumine, quod unusquisque in manu gerit.* (*Kalend.* II, p. 312). However, these things are found neither in the Greek nor in the Slavonic Typika, nor are the words of the said Psalm appropriately applied here, because according to the common interpretation they refer not to Christ's descent into Hades, but to His Ascension. *Cum hic Psalmus,* says Bellarmine, *ascensionem Domini manifeste praedicet. Quod ad Ascensionem hic Psalmus proprie pertineat, testantur Cyprianus Serm. de Ascensione, Hieronymus epistola 142 ad Damasum, Ruffinus in expositione Symboli, Gregorius Nissenus, Ioannes Chrysostomus, Augustinus, Leo, et alii in Serm. de Ascens.* [Since this Psalm manifestly foretells the Ascension of the Lord. That this Psalm properly pertains to the Ascension is attested by Cyprian, *Sermon on the Ascension*; Jerome, *Epistle 142 to Damasus*; Rufinus, *In Exposition of the Creed*; Gregory of Nyssa; John Chrysostom; Augustine; Leo; and others in their *Sermons on the Ascension*].

[^625]: That which the *Tserkovne Oko* says, and after it our Triodion and the Russian ones, that the Little Ektenia after each Ode takes place outside the Sanctuary on this Holy Day, does not agree with the Greek Triodion; for this, instead of "outside the Sanctuary", has "within the Sanctuary", *ἔσωθεν τοῦ Βήματος*, as has also the Typikon of the University of Lviv and the manuscript Slavonic Triodion which is among us. But this contradiction can be put to rest if we say that the Greek Triodion and other Typika command the Priest on this day to say all the Ektenias, and not the Deacon; and the Deacon only to carry the censer, and to pronounce the verses: **"Let God arise"**; and on this supposition the Priest sings all the Ektenias within the Sanctuary at the Holy Table. *Ἐν ἑκάστῃ δὲ Ὠδῇ γίνεται παρὰ τοῦ Ἱερέως, ἔσωθεν τοῦ Βήματος, Συναπτὴ μικρὰ* [And at each Ode there is made by the Priest, within the Sanctuary, a Little Ektenia], says the Triodion, which attributes also the other Ektenias to the Priest. For the rest, *ἔσωθεν* (within) and *ἔξωθεν* (without) differ by only a single letter, so that from this Greek copyists might easily have been deceived.

Εἶτα οἱ Ἀδελφοὶ πάντες, κατὰ τὴν τάξιν αὐτῶν, ἀσπάζονται πρῶτον τὸ ἅγιον Εὐαγγέλιον, εἶτα τὸν Ἱερέα καὶ τὸν Καθηγούμενον, καὶ ἵστανται κἀκεῖνοι ἔνθα ἂν τύχωσι, καὶ ἀσπάζονται ἀλλήλους.* [The Priest takes the holy Gospel and stands before the doors of the holy Sanctuary; and the Superior, having come and kissed the holy Gospel and the Priest, takes it from his hands and stands at the right of the Priest. In the same manner they kiss also the Priests, and among themselves according to their rank, and take their stand in a row on the right side of the Priests. Then after them the laity likewise make the kiss" (*Moscow Typikon* and *Pochaiv Triodion*, 1786).

[^634]: In the Order of the Panagia, set down in the Horologion before or after the 6th Hour, it is related that the Apostles after Christ's Resurrection, even until their dispersion throughout the whole world, dwelling with one mind in Jerusalem, had the custom to dine together, and at that time to leave an empty place at table, upon which they placed a cushion, and upon it a piece of bread for Christ's Portion, that is, in memory of Jesus Christ; and after dinner to elevate the piece of bread, saying: "Great is the name of the Holy Trinity," and: "O Lord Jesus Christ, help us"; and from the Resurrection until the Ascension: "Christ is risen." When they were doing this after the Dormition of the Most Holy Theotokos, she then appeared to them in the air in a bright cloud, alive, surrounded by Angels, saying: "Rejoice, for I am with you all the days"; and they, astonished, in place of "O Lord Jesus Christ," cried aloud: "Most Holy (*Panagía*) Theotokos, help us." This rite of the Panagia, so called from the name *Panagía*, by which the Apostles then invoked the Most Holy Theotokos, in imitation of the Apostles was used sometimes by the Emperor at Court (Codin. *De Officiis C. P.* cap. 7, in Migne, *Patrologia Graeca*, vol. 157, pp. 79–80), and by the people in churches or homes, but preeminently and daily in monasteries, as is evident from the Order of the Refectory set down in the Horologion; however, more solemnly in Bright Week, in which not a piece of the bread which they were eating, but a whole (*holóklēron*) loaf of bread they elevated throughout all the days of the Week, not partaking of it until Bright Saturday, but only kissing it. And this Order was formerly performed only in the refectory, as the Greek Pentecostarion has it; but the Slavs, for the sake of greater solemnity, did not perform this whole rite only in the refectory, but daily throughout all of Bright Week, with lamps and the Icon of the Resurrection preceding, carried the Artos from the church to the refectory, and from the refectory to the church, striking at that time all the bells, as according to the *Tserkovne Oko* our Pochaiv Triodion and Russian Typika have it. Today this Rite is performed among us only in Bright Week, and not with all the prayers and rites as the Triodion has it, but only as we have set down here in the text; however, not only in monastic churches, but in all other churches. The prayers for the Blessing and the Breaking of the Artos the Slavs added for themselves, for they are not found in the Greek books; and the prayer for the breaking is not even appointed in the Slavonic typika, except our own; while others break it without a prayer.
